author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reads a passage from Romans 8, the idea that we're not meant to live in fear like slaves, but as children who get to cry out "Abba, Father," before landing on a genuinely funny detour, everyone in the room immediately picturing the band ABBA the second the word comes up. Underneath the laughs is a real point, that we're not just children of God, we're heirs, co-heirs with Christ even, carrying the potential to be fully loved sons and daughters.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell traces his sense of purpose back to a single moment most people would never expect, a school production of Bugsy Malone when he was 15. He'd spent his childhood feeling fat, disgusting, and worthless, and was cast as Fat Sam for exactly that reason, yet the moment he stepped on stage and opened his mouth, something shifted permanently. He describes it almost physically, like tendrils falling from heaven directly into his hands, a feeling he says he's carried with him for 30 years since. He ties it to the words spoken over Christ at his baptism, "this is my son with whom I am well pleased," the first time he ever felt anything close to that kind of unconditional approval. A candid, vulnerable look back at where it all really started.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reacts to a clip of women online defending Lindsay Clancy, before pivoting into a much bigger point about how the culture creates a kind of trap, an aquarium for your consciousness, as he calls it, where whichever side of an emotional case you land on gets used against you. Sympathize with her, and that gets framed as dangerous misinformation. Condemn her outright, and that becomes the justification for banning platforms like TikTok altogether. His point isn't really about the case itself, it's that the moment you find yourself firmly on one of two suggested sides of any hot button issue, that's exactly where the culture wants you, because that's where you're easiest to manage. A genuinely thought provoking look at how outrage gets weaponized either way.
